analogy: Preparing fine-tuning data is like choosing which past exam answers to give a younger student to study. If you hand over a pile with messy answers, wrong answers and the same question copied 50 times, they'll learn the mess. If you hand over 300 neat, correct, varied ones, they'll learn the pattern. The analogy breaks because a student can tell a crossed-out wrong answer is wrong; a model copies whatever you show it, wrong answers included.

scale.title: From 1.2 million support tickets to 8,000 training examples
scale.html:
Assumptions: a telecom company has 1,200,000 resolved support tickets with agent replies and wants a model that drafts replies in house style.

  1. Exact dedup. Normalise whitespace and case, then hash. Say 18% are exact duplicates (auto-replies, copy-paste macros): 1,200,000 x 0.82 = 984,000 left.
  2. Near-dup dedup. MinHash on word shingles removes templated replies that differ only in a name or date. Say 40% go: about 590,000 left.
  3. Quality filter. Keep tickets that were resolved on the first reply and rated CSAT 4-5. Say 15% pass: about 88,500.
  4. PII scrub. Replace phone numbers, account IDs and addresses with typed placeholders like [PHONE]. Drop tickets where scrubbing breaks the meaning. Say about 80,000 remain.
  5. Stratified sample. Production traffic is 30% billing, 25% network, 20% SIM and port-out, 25% other. Sample 8,000 in those proportions, capping any single intent at 5%, so a few common intents don't drown out the rest.
  6. Group split, not random split. Split 90/10 by customer and by month, so no customer and no week of tickets sits in both train and validation. Random splitting would leak a customer's repeated issues across the split and flatter the score.
  7. Human spot-check. Read 200 random examples (2.5%). If more than 5% are bad, fix the filter and rerun, rather than hand-patching rows.

Why stop at 8,000? LIMA got strong instruction-following from just 1,000 carefully curated examples (arXiv 2305.11206). Curation beats volume.

lab.look_for: Open the lab's tiny training set and check that each example has the same structure the model will see at inference. Duplicate one example 20 times and retrain: training loss drops faster, but the model starts parroting that one answer, a small version of the duplication problem in this lesson. The lab's data is toy-sized, so judge the direction of the change, not the numbers.

quiz.q: You randomly split 50,000 tickets 90/10. Many customers filed 5-10 near-identical tickets. Validation accuracy is 94%; on next month's tickets it's 78%. What is the most likely cause?

options.t: Group leakage: the same customers' near-identical tickets landed in both train and validation, so validation rewarded memorisation.
options.why: Correct. Split by group (customer, thread, time window) so related examples stay on one side. Random row-level splits leak whenever rows are correlated.

options.t: The model is too small for the task.
options.why: A capacity problem would show low validation scores too. A high validation score that collapses on fresh data is the signature of leakage.

options.t: Next month's tickets are harder; nothing is wrong with the evaluation.
options.why: Possible but unproven. The correlated-rows setup makes leakage the first thing to rule out, and a time-based split would test this directly.

options.t: Too few epochs.
options.why: More training would increase memorisation, widening the gap rather than closing it.

exercises.q: You have 10,000 rows. 22% are exact duplicates; of the rest, 30% are near-duplicates; 20% of what remains fails your quality filter. How many examples are left?
exercises.a: 10,000 x 0.78 = 7,800. 7,800 x 0.70 = 5,460. 5,460 x 0.80 = 4,368. Each filter multiplies, which is why raw counts badly overstate usable data. Plan your collection around the final number.

exercises.q: Your examples come from three teams: one writes 'Hi there,' and bullet lists, one writes formal paragraphs, one writes one-liners. You want one consistent house style. What do you do with the data?
exercises.a: Pick the target style and write it down with 5 gold examples. Then either keep only the examples that already match (if there are enough), or rewrite the others into the target style, by people or with a strong model plus human review, and record which examples are rewritten. Mixed styles in training teach the model to pick a style at random, which looks like inconsistency in production. Check with a style rubric on validation outputs.

exercises.q: Design a pipeline that keeps the fine-tuning set fresh: production failures should flow back in each month without contaminating the eval set.
exercises.a: Log production outputs with user feedback and reviewer corrections. Each month, sample failures and corrections, scrub PII, and send them through the same dedup and quality filters. Before adding, run near-dup matching against the frozen eval set and drop any candidate too close to an eval item. Keep the eval set frozen and versioned, with a small new eval slice each quarter for drift, kept separately. Version the training set (hash plus manifest) per model release so any result can be reproduced, and track the training mix by intent so new data doesn't skew it.

interview.q: What makes a good fine-tuning dataset?
interview.a: Consistent format that matches exactly how the model will be prompted in production, including the system message and chat template. High-quality target outputs, because the model copies them. Coverage of the real input distribution, including edge cases, without a few common cases dominating. Deduplicated and clean. And a validation split that is truly held out. A few hundred to a few thousand excellent examples usually beat a much larger noisy set; LIMA used 1,000.

interview.q: How do you prevent train/validation leakage in practice?
interview.a: First, dedupe across the split, not just within it, with near-duplicate detection such as MinHash or embedding similarity, since exact hashing misses templated text. Second, split by group: customer, conversation thread, document or time window, so correlated examples stay together. For anything that will run on future data, a time-based split is the most honest. Third, freeze the eval set and check every new training batch against it. Finally, if the score looks too good, measure on a fresh sample of production data before believing it.

interview.q: You can buy 100,000 synthetic examples generated by a frontier model, or spend the same budget on 3,000 expert-written examples. How do you decide?
interview.a: Run a small pilot of both against the same eval. Synthetic data is good for coverage and format but carries the generator's errors, biases and sameness, and some providers' terms restrict training on their outputs, so I'd check the license. Expert data is better for the hard, high-stakes cases. Often the best mix is a few thousand expert examples as the core, plus synthetic data that has been filtered and graded to fill coverage gaps, with every synthetic example passing an automatic check and a sample passing human review. The decision should come from eval results per slice, not from volume.

analogy: LoRA is like putting clip-on lenses over a camera instead of rebuilding it. The camera (the frozen base model) stays exactly as it was; the small clip-on (the adapter) bends the picture the way you want, and you can swap clip-ons for different jobs. QLoRA is the same, but you also pack the camera body into a smaller case (4-bit) so it fits in your bag. The analogy breaks because a clip-on can't add a feature the camera lacks; LoRA can steer what the model can already do, but it is a poor way to pour in new facts.

scale.title: LoRA math for Qwen2.5-7B: parameters, memory and 12 department adapters
scale.html:
From the model's config.json: hidden size 3,584, MLP size 18,944, 28 layers, 28 query heads and 4 key/value heads of size 128 (so k and v project to 512). The model card lists 7.61B parameters.

  1. LoRA on one matrix. A weight W of shape d_out x d_in gets B (d_out x r) and A (r x d_in), so r x (d_in + d_out) trainable parameters. The update is W + (alpha/r) x BA, and B starts at zero, so training starts from the unchanged model (LoRA, arXiv 2106.09685; PEFT's default init).
  2. One layer, r = 16, all linear layers. q and o: 16 x (3,584 + 3,584) = 114,688 each. k and v: 16 x (3,584 + 512) = 65,536 each. gate and up: 16 x (3,584 + 18,944) = 360,448 each. down: 360,448. Layer total = 1,441,792.
  3. Whole model. 1,441,792 x 28 = 40,370,176 trainable parameters, about 0.53% of 7.61B. Adapter file: about 81 MB in bf16, 161 MB in fp32. (q and v only, the LoRA paper's main setting: about 5.0M, 0.07%.)
  4. Memory. Full fine-tuning at about 18 bytes per parameter (HF memory guide) = 137 GB. QLoRA: the frozen base in 4-bit NF4 is about 0.5 bytes per parameter = 3.8 GB (plus small quantization constants, which QLoRA's double quantization shrinks), and the 40.4M adapter parameters at 18 bytes = 0.73 GB, plus activations. The QLoRA paper fit a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU (arXiv 2305.14314).
  5. 12 departments. 12 full copies in bf16 = 12 x 15.2 GB = 183 GB. One base + 12 adapters = 15.2 GB + 12 x 81 MB = about 16.2 GB.

lab.look_for: The first half prints the LoRA parameter math for the real Qwen2.5-7B config; check that its totals match this page's 40,370,176 at r = 16 on all linear layers, then change r to 8 and target modules to q and v only and watch the count drop. The second half trains a real adapter on a tiny model: note the 'trainable %' line and the adapter's size on disk next to the base model's.

quiz.q: A LoRA adapter on a 4,096 x 4,096 weight matrix with rank r = 8 adds how many trainable parameters?

options.why: Correct. r x (d_in + d_out) = 8 x (4,096 + 4,096) = 65,536, against 16,777,216 in the frozen matrix: 0.39%.
That's r x 4,096, counting only one of the two matrices. LoRA trains both A (r x d_in) and B (d_out x r).
That's the full matrix, which LoRA freezes. The point is to train far fewer parameters than this.
That would be rank 16. Parameter count grows linearly with r.

quiz.q: Which statement about QLoRA is accurate?

options.t: It freezes the base model in 4-bit NF4 and backpropagates through it into LoRA adapters that train in higher precision; it also uses double quantization and paged optimizers to save memory.
options.why: Correct. That is the recipe in Dettmers et al. (arXiv 2305.14314): a 4-bit frozen base, 16-bit-quality results, and memory tricks that fit a 65B model on one 48 GB GPU.

options.t: It trains the 4-bit weights directly, so the base model itself changes.
options.why: The quantized base stays frozen. Only the LoRA adapters receive updates.

options.t: It makes inference 4x faster because the adapter is in 4-bit.
options.why: QLoRA is a training-memory technique. 4-bit inference speed depends on kernels and hardware, and the adapter isn't the 4-bit part.

options.t: It needs no training data because the quantization does the adapting.
options.why: Quantization only compresses the frozen base. Behaviour still comes from training the adapter on your data.

exercises.q: Compute LoRA trainable parameters for a model with hidden size 2,048, MLP size 8,192, 24 layers, full-width k and v (no grouped-query attention), r = 8 on all seven linear layers per block.
Your QLoRA fine-tune for a support-reply style works, but answers about product specs got worse. A teammate suggests raising r from 16 to 128 to 'learn the specs'. What do you say?
exercises.a: Wrong lever. Product specs are knowledge that changes; that is RAG's job, and fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts. The drop in spec answers is likely forgetting or style override from training. Check whether training examples contained wrong or outdated specs. Fix it by keeping r modest, adding general and spec-grounded examples where the answer comes from retrieved context (so the model learns to use context rather than memorise), and measuring both the style metric and spec accuracy against the base model. Biderman et al. found LoRA forgets less than full fine-tuning, but it isn't zero.

exercises.q: You serve 40 customer-specific LoRA adapters on one 7B base. Traffic is skewed: 3 adapters get 70% of requests. Design serving and deployment.
exercises.a: Keep one base model in GPU memory and load adapters dynamically; use a server that batches requests for different adapters together (the S-LoRA line of work, arXiv 2311.03285, showed thousands of adapters on one GPU). Keep the 3 hot adapters resident and load the long tail from CPU memory or disk on demand with an LRU cache. Consider merging an adapter into a dedicated deployment (PEFT's merge_and_unload) only if a tenant needs isolation or the lowest latency. Version adapters with the base model hash, since an adapter is only valid for the exact base it was trained on. Run each adapter's eval before promoting it, and roll out per tenant.

interview.q: Explain LoRA in plain terms.
interview.a: Instead of updating a huge weight matrix W during fine-tuning, LoRA freezes W and learns a small low-rank update: two thin matrices B and A whose product has the same shape as W. The output becomes Wx plus a scaled BAx. Because r is small (8, 16, 64), you train a tiny fraction of the parameters, often well under 1%. The LoRA paper reported 10,000x fewer trainable parameters and 3x less GPU memory than full fine-tuning on GPT-3 175B, with on-par quality on their benchmarks. You can merge the update into W afterwards, so there's no extra inference latency.

interview.q: How do you choose r, alpha and target modules?
interview.a: Start with sensible defaults and let the eval decide. Target modules: all linear layers is a strong default (QLoRA applied adapters to all linear layers, and PEFT supports 'all-linear'); attention-only is lighter. Rank: 8-16 for style and format, higher for harder tasks, raising it only if the model underfits on validation. Alpha scales the update by alpha/r; many people keep alpha around r to 2r, and rsLoRA scales by alpha over the square root of r so higher ranks behave more stably. Learning rate matters more than people expect: adapters usually use around 1e-4 to 2e-4. Then sweep a couple of settings on a held-out set.

interview.q: When would you choose full fine-tuning over LoRA?
interview.a: When the target needs a large change to the model and you have the data and compute: continued pretraining on a new domain or language, or heavy instruction tuning with hundreds of thousands of examples. Biderman et al. found LoRA substantially underperformed full fine-tuning on code and math in those regimes, while forgetting less of the base model's other abilities, and that full fine-tuning learns updates of much higher rank. For most product work (style, format, a narrow task, many tenant variants), LoRA wins on cost, iteration speed and serving. The choice is driven by an eval on both target and general ability.

analogy: Instruction tuning is like teaching a parrot that already knows thousands of words how to answer questions instead of just repeating whatever it hears. You show it again and again: when someone asks this, the answer looks like that. Preference tuning is then giving it a treat for the better of two answers. The analogy breaks because a parrot learns from the treat in the moment, while a model learns only from what's in the examples, including their mistakes and their formatting tokens.

scale.title: Instruction-tuning a support model on 8,000 conversations
scale.html:
Assumptions: 8,000 curated support conversations (from Lesson 5.3). Each has a system message (150 tokens), a customer message (350 tokens) and an agent reply (250 tokens): 750 tokens per example.

  1. Tokens per epoch. 8,000 x 750 = 6 million tokens. Three epochs = 18 million.
  2. Which tokens carry the loss? TRL computes loss on the whole sequence for a conversational (messages) dataset unless you set assistant_only_loss=True; for prompt-completion datasets it uses completion-only loss by default (TRL SFT docs). With full-sequence loss, only 250 / 750 = 33% of the loss comes from the replies you want to teach; the rest teaches the model to predict system prompts and customer messages.
  3. Switch to assistant-only loss. 8,000 x 250 = 2 million loss-carrying tokens per epoch, all of them reply behaviour. TRL notes this needs a chat template with generation markers, which it patches automatically for some known families.
  4. Template and EOS. Qwen2.5 models use <|im_start|> and <|im_end|> turn markers. TRL's docs warn that for a base model like Qwen2.5-1.5B you should set eos_token="<|im_end|>" so replies stop where the template says the turn ends. Skip that, and the model may keep generating past the reply.
  5. Then maybe preference tuning. If reviewers can easily say which of two replies is better but can't write the perfect reply, collect 2,000 preference pairs and run DPO (arXiv 2305.18290) on top of the SFT checkpoint.

lab.look_for: Print one tokenised training example and find where the prompt ends and the response begins; check which positions have label -100 (ignored) and which carry loss. Then generate from the trained adapter with the same template and with a different one, and compare: the mismatch is this lesson's chat-template gotcha at toy scale.

quiz.q: You SFT on conversational 'messages' data with TRL defaults. What does the loss cover?

options.t: The full sequence, including system and user turns, unless you set assistant_only_loss=True (which needs generation markers in the chat template).
options.why: Correct. Per the TRL docs, assistant_only_loss defaults to False; completion-only loss is the default only for prompt-completion datasets. Turn on assistant-only loss to focus learning on the replies.

options.t: Only the assistant turns, always.
options.why: That's what many people assume, but it isn't the default for messages datasets in TRL. Check your config.

options.t: Only the system prompt.
options.why: No standard setup trains on just the system prompt.

options.t: Nothing until you add a reward model.
options.why: SFT uses plain next-token cross-entropy on its targets; reward models belong to RLHF.

exercises.q: An example has 120 system tokens, 400 user tokens and 180 assistant tokens. What fraction of loss-carrying tokens is assistant behaviour with full-sequence loss, and with assistant-only loss?
exercises.a: Full sequence: 180 / (120 + 400 + 180) = 180 / 700 = 25.7%. Assistant-only: 100% of loss-carrying tokens are assistant tokens, and there are 180 of them. With long prompts and short answers, full-sequence loss spends most of the gradient on text you never want the model to generate.

exercises.q: Your SFT model gives good answers but then keeps going, inventing a new 'user:' turn and answering it. What's wrong and how do you fix it?
exercises.a: The model never learned where a turn ends: the end-of-turn token in the template doesn't match the EOS token used in training or generation. Fix: make the tokenizer's eos_token the template's end-of-turn token (for Qwen2.5, <|im_end|>, which TRL's docs call out), make sure each training example ends with it, and pass it as a stop token at inference. Re-check by decoding a training example and looking at its last tokens.

exercises.q: You have budget for either 5,000 more SFT examples or 5,000 preference pairs. The model's replies are accurate but often too long and slightly off in tone. Which do you buy, and how do you set it up?
exercises.a: Preference pairs suit this case. The model already knows what to say; the problem is a subtle quality judgement (length, tone) that is easier to compare than to write perfectly. Generate two replies per prompt from the SFT model, have reviewers pick the better one by a written rubric (concise, warm, accurate), and run DPO starting from the SFT checkpoint with the same chat template. Evaluate reply length, rubric scores and accuracy against the SFT model, since preference tuning can trade accuracy for style if pairs reward tone alone. If the issue were missing knowledge or wrong format, more SFT would be the right buy.

interview.q: What is the difference between SFT, RLHF and DPO?
interview.a: SFT trains on input-output demonstrations with next-token cross-entropy: the model imitates the good answers. RLHF, as in InstructGPT, trains a reward model on human rankings of outputs, then optimises the policy with reinforcement learning to score highly on that reward while staying close to the original model. DPO gets a similar effect directly from preferred-versus-rejected pairs with a classification-style loss and no separate reward model or RL loop, which makes it simpler and more stable to run. In practice: SFT first, then DPO if you have preference data and a quality gap that demonstrations don't fix.

interview.q: What is a chat template and how does it break fine-tunes?
interview.a: A chat template is the exact text format, with special tokens, that turns a list of messages into the token sequence a model was trained on. For Qwen it uses im_start and im_end markers around each role. If training data is formatted with one template and inference with another, or the end-of-turn token isn't the EOS token, the model sees unfamiliar input. You get degraded answers, or replies that never stop and start inventing turns. I always format with the tokenizer's apply_chat_template, decode a training sample to check it by eye, and serve with the same template and stop tokens.

interview.q: Design an instruction-tuning project to turn a base model into an internal coding assistant for your company's frameworks.
interview.a: Start with an instruct model, not a raw base, unless there's a strong reason, since it already follows instructions. Data: mine real internal questions and accepted answers from code review and support channels, plus expert-written examples for core frameworks, deduped and split by repository and time. Include examples that use retrieved docs in context, so the model learns to rely on RAG for API details instead of memorising them. Train LoRA SFT with assistant-only loss and the model's own chat template. Evaluate on held-out internal tasks with tests that execute, plus general coding and safety probes against the base. Add DPO later from developer thumbs-up and thumbs-down data. Version the adapter with the base model.

analogy: Evaluating a fine-tune is like checking whether extra maths tuition helped a student. You don't ask the tutor; you give the student a test they haven't seen. You also check they didn't forget how to read while cramming maths. The analogy breaks because a student's school report covers many subjects for free; for a model, you only find out what got worse if you built a test for it.

scale.title: Is 0.60 to 0.91 real, and did general ability drop?
scale.html:
Assumptions: a held-out task set of 1,000 examples and a general-ability probe of 300 diverse prompts. Base model: 0.60 on the task, 0.82 on the probe. Fine-tune: 0.91 on the task, 0.76 on the probe.

  1. Task gain uncertainty. Standard error of a proportion = sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Tuned: sqrt(0.91 x 0.09 / 1,000) = 0.009, so the 95% interval is about +/-1.8 points. Base: sqrt(0.60 x 0.40 / 1,000) = 0.015, about +/-3.0 points. A 31-point gain is far outside both: real.
  2. General drop uncertainty. Base: sqrt(0.82 x 0.18 / 300) = 0.022. Tuned: sqrt(0.76 x 0.24 / 300) = 0.025. Standard error of the difference, treating them as independent, is about sqrt(0.022^2 + 0.025^2) = 0.033. The 6-point drop is about 1.8 standard errors: suggestive but not conclusive.
  3. Use a paired test. Both models answered the same 300 prompts, so count disagreements. Say 31 prompts flipped from right to wrong and 13 from wrong to right: net 18 / 300 = 6 points. McNemar's statistic = (31 - 13)^2 / (31 + 13) = 324 / 44 = 7.4, above 3.84 (the 5% threshold), so the drop is real.
  4. Diagnose. Read the 31 regressions. Say most are 'ignores instructions to answer in a list': the fine-tune overwrote format-following.
  5. Fix and re-measure. Mix 10% general instruction data into training, cut epochs from 3 to 2, and re-run both sets. Biderman et al. report LoRA forgets less than full fine-tuning, but it still forgets (arXiv 2405.09673).

lab.look_for: The regression gate compares two versions case by case, which is exactly 'fine-tune versus base on the same held-out set'. Look at the per-case table, not just the totals: count cases that went from pass to fail as well as fail to pass. Swap in your base and tuned outputs as the two versions, and check whether the position-bias test changes your judge's verdicts.

quiz.q: On 300 shared probe prompts, 25 flip from right to wrong after fine-tuning and 25 flip from wrong to right. What do you conclude?

options.t: Net general accuracy is unchanged, but the model's behaviour changed on 50 prompts, so read those flips to see what moved.
options.why: Correct. Equal flips give the same total, but a 17% change in which prompts pass is a real behaviour shift; the totals hide it. The 25 new failures may matter more (safety, key customers) than the 25 new passes.

options.t: Nothing changed; ship it.
options.why: Totals can stay flat while behaviour changes a lot. Look at what flipped before shipping.

options.t: The fine-tune is clearly worse.
options.why: The counts are balanced; there's no net loss. Whether it's worse depends on which prompts flipped.

options.t: The probe set is broken because results changed.
options.why: Changing results are what a probe is for. The set isn't broken; you need to read the flipped cases.

exercises.q: Your held-out set has 200 examples. The base scores 0.70 and the fine-tune 0.75. Roughly how big is the 95% interval on each score, and is the gain convincing?
exercises.a: SE(0.70) = sqrt(0.7 x 0.3 / 200) = 0.032, so about +/-6.4 points. SE(0.75) = sqrt(0.75 x 0.25 / 200) = 0.031, about +/-6.0 points. The intervals overlap heavily; a 5-point gain on 200 examples isn't convincing on its own. Run a paired test on the per-example flips, or grow the set. Small eval sets make fine-tunes look better or worse at random.

exercises.q: Your fine-tune passes the offline eval, but after launch users report it refuses harmless requests more often. Which eval was missing, and how do you add it?
exercises.a: A safety and over-refusal probe. Build two sets: harmful requests the model must refuse, and borderline-but-harmless requests it must answer (medical information, security education, fiction). Score refusal rates on both for base and tuned models, and gate releases on both: refusals of harmful requests must not drop, and refusals of harmless ones must not rise beyond a set threshold. Training data often contains many refusals or hedged replies that teach over-caution, so check the dataset for that too.

exercises.q: Write a release gate for fine-tuned adapters that runs in CI. List the suites, the metrics and the pass rules.
exercises.a: Suites: (1) frozen held-out task set; (2) general-ability probe; (3) safety: must-refuse and must-answer; (4) format and contract tests (valid JSON, schema, stops correctly); (5) a slice of last month's real traffic with reference answers. Metrics: task score with confidence interval, paired flips against the current production adapter, refusal rates, format failure rate, latency and tokens per answer. Pass rules: task score not lower than production (paired test), general probe net flips not significantly negative, harmful-refusal rate not lower, harmless-refusal rate up no more than 1 point, zero format regressions. Store all outputs so failures can be read, and require human sign-off for any rule override.

interview.q: How do you know a fine-tune actually helped?
interview.a: I compare it with the base model, and with the best prompt-only setup, on a held-out set it never trained on, using a task metric that reflects what users need. I check that the gain is bigger than the noise for the set size, ideally with a paired comparison since both models see the same examples. Then I check it didn't get worse elsewhere: a general-ability probe, safety refusals and format compliance. Only if the target improved and the guardrail metrics held do I call it a win. After launch, I confirm with an A/B test or a staged rollout.

interview.q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you detect and reduce it?
interview.a: It's when training on a narrow task makes the model worse at things it used to do: following general instructions, reasoning, formatting or safety behaviour. You detect it by running probes outside the target task on both base and tuned models and comparing per prompt, not just averages. To reduce it: train less aggressively (fewer epochs, lower learning rate), use LoRA, which Biderman et al. found forgets less than full fine-tuning, mix some general instruction data into the training set, and keep the rank modest. Then re-measure both axes.

interview.q: Leadership wants one number to decide if the fine-tune ships. What do you give them?
interview.a: I'd push back gently: one number hides trade-offs. But I can give one decision with a short scorecard behind it. The headline is the change in the business metric's proxy, for example 'resolution-quality score up 9 points (95% CI 6 to 12) versus production'. Under it, three guardrails with pass or fail: general ability held, safety refusals held, cost and latency within budget. If any guardrail fails, the answer is no regardless of the headline. Then a rollout plan: 5% traffic for a week, watching live metrics, with automatic rollback.
